newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel signals compromise on tax-reform plan-paper.
newsitem.headline: Waigel signals compromise on tax-reform plan-paper.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday signaled the government would be willing to reduce social security contributions as part of a compromise to push through an ambitious tax-reform package.
"We are also willing to cut social security contributions by about one point and finance this by raising indirect taxes," Waigel told mass circulation paper Bild in an interview.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democrats and junior coalition parter Free Democrats plan to resume talks with the opposition Social Democrats on a massive tax-reform package next Tuesday.

Setting his side's mood for next week's talks, Waigel told the newspaper, "I am willing to compromise. Germany needs this tax-reform so that the jobless rate can be reduced permanently. But of course both sides need to approach one another in such talks."
But Waigel also said the government would stick by plans to cut two points off the 7.5 percent solidarity tax on January 1, 1998 despite calls from the opposition to postpone the cut.
The unpopular tax was designed to finance German unification.

The Social Democrats have called for speedy cuts in private taxes, particularly the high social security contributions to pay for unemployment insurance and pensions and have suggested these be financed through higher value-added-taxes or oil and gas taxes.

"Our plans also include a cut in taxes for individuals beginning January 1, 1998, by cutting the solidarity tax by more than one quarter. With this we continue on our course of tax reductions," Waigel said.

Tax-reform plans have taken on particular importance as Germany scrambles to meet the strict fiscal criteria set down in the Maastricht Treaty so that it can be among the first group of nations to join Europe's currency union in 1999.
